opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The headline result, I'd say, is that diffusion is a genuinely competitive way to train language models, not just a curiosity. For a long time the assumption was that autoregression, predicting one token at a time left to right, was simply the right way to model text, and that diffusion worked for images but wouldn't carry over to discrete data like language. What we found is that once you set up the discrete diffusion objective properly, in a way that respects the structure of discrete tokens rather than forcing continuous-space ideas onto them, you can get quality in the same ballpark as autoregressive models trained at comparable scale.

The more interesting part is what you get beyond matching quality. Because a diffusion model refines the whole sequence in parallel over a number of denoising steps, you're no longer bottlenecked by generating tokens strictly one after another. That opens up a different speed-quality trade-off. You can choose how many refinement steps to spend, and in practice you can generate much faster on modern hardware, which is very good at parallel computation and less efficient at sequential decoding.

There's also a modeling angle. An autoregressive model commits to each token and can't go back. A diffusion model can revise earlier parts of the output as it goes, and it naturally conditions on context in both directions. That helps with things like infilling and editing, and potentially with tasks where you'd like to plan the overall structure before filling in details.

So the key takeaway for me is that autoregression isn't the only viable path. Diffusion holds up on quality, and it brings real advantages in speed, controllability, and flexibility. That's why we think it's worth seriously investing in as an alternative paradigm for language generation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, great to be here. The headline result for me is that diffusion-based language models and autoregressive models are actually much closer in terms of what you can get out of a given training budget than most people assumed. For years the folklore was that autoregressive is the only recipe that scales for text, and diffusion is this thing that works for images but doesn't really belong in the language world. What we found when we did a careful, apples-to-apples comparison is that the gap is mostly a gap in how well each paradigm has been engineered, not something fundamental.

Concretely, we trained both families of models under matched conditions, same data, same compute, same parameter counts, and looked at how the loss and downstream quality scaled. Diffusion models follow a scaling law that looks very much like the autoregressive one. They're somewhat less efficient per token at the moment, so you pay a modest premium in compute to reach the same likelihood, but that premium has been shrinking as we've improved the training objective and the noise schedule. And importantly, it's a constant-factor difference, not a difference in the exponent, which means it's the kind of gap that engineering closes over time.

The second part of the story, and honestly the part I find more exciting, is what you get for that premium. Because a diffusion model isn't locked into a left-to-right ordering, you can generate tokens in parallel, you can do in-filling and editing natively, and you can trade off compute at inference time for quality in a way that's very hard to do with a standard decoder. So the paper's real message is that the dominance of autoregressive modeling has been partly a historical accident. There's a legitimate second path for building language models, and it has its own set of advantages that are worth taking seriously.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame the key result as a distinction between the model’s factorization and the way we train it. Autoregressive training gives you a very natural task: predict the next token from the prefix. Diffusion training exposes the model to a range of prediction problems, reconstructing tokens from partially corrupted context.

So when we compare them, we’re also comparing different ways of using the training data and allocating computation. The interesting question isn’t just which model generates better text, but how much of that difference comes from the training objective. I wouldn’t take it as a blanket statement that diffusion is better than autoregression; it’s a reason to look more carefully at what makes each approach effective.
